title: Python: Functions, Data & Files
intro: This term your Python grows muscles: functions, lists, dictionaries and files that remember data. You will build a market price tracker that saves prices and never crashes on bad entries.
termProject: Oja Price Tracker: a Python tool that records market prices (tomatoes, pepper, garri, rice) into a CSV file day by day, then reports cheapest, dearest and average prices and safely skips bad entries.
generatedNote: Weeks 1-3 were not defined in the official ByteBusters curriculum. They were designed by Claude (AI) as a bridge from Year 2 Term 3 to Week 4, for review by the ByteBusters team and head office.

weeks.unit: Weeks 1-3 · Python Foundations Bridge (proposed by Claude)
weeks.title: Loops that do the work
weeks.goal: Use for with range and a while loop to repeat work instead of typing it many times.
weeks.learn: Ajo savings means putting money aside every day. Writing 30 lines for 30 days is tiring, so we use loops. A for loop with range repeats a known number of times, like 7 days of the week. A while loop keeps going until a condition is false, like saving until you reach your target. Always make sure a while loop can stop.

research.q: Ask someone who does ajo or esusu: how much do they save daily and for how many days?
research.tip: Use their real pattern (not their name) to set daily and target in your code.

build.task: Print a 7-day savings table with for, then count days to reach a target with while.
steps: Type the code into ajo.py
Run and read the 7-day table
Change daily to 300 and target to 6000
Predict the number of days before running
build.code:
daily = 200
total = 0

for day in range(1, 8):
    total = total + daily
    print("Day", day, ": saved", total, "naira")

target = 5000
saved = 0
days = 0
while saved < target:
    saved = saved + daily
    days = days + 1

print("You reach", target, "naira in", days, "days")

check.q: When does a while loop stop?
Which loop is best when you don't know how many rounds?

weeks.say: I learnt that for loops repeat a set number of times and while loops repeat until a condition is false.

weeks.title: Strings and simple lists
weeks.goal: Clean up text with string methods and keep many items in one list.
weeks.learn: A string is text, like a shopping item. Methods like strip(), title() and upper() clean and style it. A list is like a market basket: one name holding many items, in order. You can add with append(), count with len(), and loop through every item. This bridge gets you ready for functions and data structures next week.

weeks.title: Functions: little machines
weeks.goal: Write functions with arguments, default values and return, and understand scope.
weeks.learn: A function is like a grinding machine at the market: you put in pepper (arguments), it works, and gives you ground pepper back (return). def makes the function and you can use it many times. A default argument is a normal setting you can change. Variables made inside a function stay inside it; that is called scope.

research.q: Ask a trader: what calculation do you do again and again every day?
research.tip: That repeated calculation is a perfect function, like adding delivery or giving change.

build.task: Write a function that adds delivery to a price and another that describes an item nicely.
steps: Type the code into functions.py
Run it and read the two answers
Call price_with_delivery with your own numbers
Uncomment the last line to see the scope error, then comment it back
build.code:
def price_with_delivery(price, delivery=500):
    total = price + delivery
    return total

def describe(item, price):
    full = price_with_delivery(price)
    return f"{item}: ₦{full:,} with delivery"

print(describe("Bag of garri", 9000))
print(price_with_delivery(2000, delivery=0))

# Scope: 'total' only lives inside price_with_delivery.
# print(total)   # NameError: name 'total' is not defined

opts: Sends an answer back to the caller

check.q: Why does print(total) outside the function fail?
opts: total only exists inside the function

weeks.say: I learnt that a function is a little machine: it takes arguments, does work and returns an answer.

weeks.title: Lists and tuples: rows of prices
weeks.goal: Store prices in a list, sort and summarise them, and use a tuple for fixed data.
weeks.learn: A list can change: you can add, remove and sort, like prices that change every market day. A tuple uses round brackets and cannot change, like a market's name and its state. sum(), len(), min() and max() quickly summarise numbers. enumerate() gives you the position and the item together.

research.q: Ask two sellers the price of the same item (for example a paint bucket of tomatoes) on the same day.
research.tip: Write both prices; different sellers give different prices, which is why we compare.

build.task: Store this week's practice tomato prices, then find the cheapest, dearest and average.
steps: Type the code into prices.py
Run and read the summary
Put in prices from your research
Try changing the tuple and read the error
build.code:
prices = [1200, 1500, 900, 1800]   # practice prices for tomatoes this week
prices.append(1300)
prices.sort()

print("Cheapest:", prices[0], "Dearest:", prices[-1])
print("Average:", round(sum(prices) / len(prices)))

market = ("Ilaro Market", "Ogun State")   # tuple: fixed, cannot change
name, state = market
print(name, "is in", state)
# market[0] = "Oja Oba"   # TypeError: tuples cannot be changed

for i, p in enumerate(prices, start=1):
    print(i, "->", p, "naira")

check.q: Which one can be changed after it is made?

weeks.say: I learnt that lists are for data that changes and tuples are for data that stays fixed.

weeks.title: Dictionaries: the shop's stock book

research.q: Ask a shopkeeper: how do you know when an item has finished and you must restock?
research.tip: Their rule (for example 'below 3 bags') becomes an if in your stock checker.

weeks.title: Files: Python's notebook
weeks.goal: Write market prices into a text file and read them back line by line.
weeks.learn: When a program ends, its variables vanish, like chalk wiped from the board. A file is a notebook that keeps data even after the program stops. open() with 'w' writes a new file, and 'r' reads it. Using with closes the file for you, like closing your notebook after writing.

research.q: Ask a trader: do you write your sales or prices down? Where, and why?
research.tip: This shows why saving data matters; a program that forgets is like a seller with no notebook.

build.task: Save three practice prices into prices.txt, then read and print them nicely.
steps: Type the code into notebook.py
Run it; a file prices.txt appears
Open prices.txt to see what was written
Add two items from your research and run again
build.code:
# Write a new file (w = write, it replaces old content)
with open("prices.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("tomatoes,1200\n")
    f.write("pepper,800\n")
    f.write("onions,600\n")

# Read it back line by line
with open("prices.txt", "r") as f:
    for line in f:
        item, price = line.strip().split(",")
        print(item.title(), "costs ₦" + price)

check.q: Which mode writes a new file?

opts: It closes the file for you

weeks.say: I learnt that files keep data after a program stops, and Python can write and read them.

weeks.title: CSV files: a price diary
weeks.goal: Append each day's price to a CSV file and read the whole diary back.
weeks.learn: CSV means comma-separated values; it opens in Excel or Google Sheets like a table. Mode 'a' (append) adds new lines at the end without wiping old ones, like adding a new day in a diary. Python's csv module writes and reads rows safely. date.today() stamps each entry with the day.

research.q: Ask a trader: which day of the week are prices usually cheapest, and why?
research.tip: Record their answer; later your price diary can check if it is true.

build.task: Add today's practice price to market.csv every time the program runs, then print the diary.
steps: Type the code into diary.py
Run it three times
Open market.csv and see three rows
Change the item and price, run again
build.code:
import csv
from datetime import date

item = "tomatoes"
price = 1300   # practice price

# a = append: add to the end, keep old rows
with open("market.csv", "a", newline="") as f:
    writer = csv.writer(f)
    writer.writerow([date.today(), item, price])

with open("market.csv", newline="") as f:
    for row in csv.reader(f):
        print(row[0], "|", row[1], "| ₦" + row[2])

check.q: Which mode adds without wiping old data?

weeks.say: I learnt that append mode adds new rows to a CSV file so my price diary grows every day.

trainer.open: A trader who remembers last week's price can bargain better. Let's give our program memory across days!

weeks.title: Exceptions: don't crash, handle it
weeks.goal: Use try/except/finally to handle missing files and bad numbers without crashing.
weeks.learn: Real data is messy: someone types 'two thousand' instead of 2000, or the file is missing. An error that stops the program is called an exception. try runs risky code, except catches a named problem and does something sensible, and finally always runs. It is like a danfo driver who keeps a spare tyre: a flat tyre does not end the journey.

research.q: Ask someone who handles records (a teacher, cashier or POS agent): what mistakes do people make when writing numbers?
research.tip: Each mistake is a test case you should feed into your program.

weeks.title: Bug hunting: debug like a mechanic
weeks.goal: Read an error message, find the bug with prints, fix it and prove it with assert tests.
weeks.learn: A mechanic listens to the engine, finds the faulty part, fixes it and test-drives the car. Debugging is the same. Read the last line of the error first: it names the problem and the line. Use print to see what values really are. assert checks that an answer is what you expect, so the same bug never comes back quietly.

research.q: Ask a mechanic, phone repairer or tailor: how do you find out what is wrong before you fix it?
research.tip: Write their steps down; they are almost the same steps programmers use.
